fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I keep going back and forth on, honestly. Let me try to separate two things, because I think people blur them together.

One is perception. Recognizing objects, segmenting, captioning an image. For that, I don't think you need a world model in any serious sense. You need a good representation, good data, and scale. That's basically what we've been doing for the last ten years, and it works.

The other is acting. The moment the system has to do something and then live with the consequences, you need some ability to predict what happens next. If I push this cup, does it tip over? If the car in front of me brakes, where will I be in two seconds? That's where I think a vision world model becomes not just nice to have, but essential. Robotics, driving, any kind of embodied agent. You can't collect enough real interaction data to cover all those cases, so the model has to carry its own simulator inside it.

And I'd actually push this a bit further. Even for things that look like pure reasoning, like a model trying to solve a physics problem from a diagram, I think the models that do well are the ones that have some internal notion of how things move and interact. It doesn't have to be a pixel-level video predictor. It can be pretty abstract. But there's a difference between knowing the word "gravity" and having a prior that things fall.

What I'm less sure about is the current form. A lot of what gets called a world model right now is really a video generation model, and generating plausible frames is not the same as predicting the right frame for the purpose of making a decision. Those objectives can diverge. So I think the need is real, but I'm not convinced we've found the right way to train for it yet.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on what kind of work we mean.

For a large share of knowledge work, like writing code, proving theorems, drafting documents, or answering questions, I'm not convinced you need a vision world model at all. Language is a very compressed and very powerful interface, and these tasks live almost entirely in text or symbols. Language models already show you can get remarkably far there without ever seeing a pixel.

But once the work touches the physical world, I think a vision world model becomes close to necessary. Robotics is the obvious case. If you want a robot to fold laundry, cook, or assemble something, it has to predict what happens when it pushes this object or grasps that one. It has to know whether something will slide, tip over, or deform. Very little of that knowledge is written down anywhere. Nobody writes a paragraph describing exactly how a towel drapes when you lift one corner. That kind of intuitive physics is in the visual world, not in text, so you have to learn it from seeing.

The other reason is planning and safety. In the physical world you can't just try things a million times the way you can in a simulator or a code sandbox. Trial and error is expensive and sometimes dangerous. So you want a model that can imagine: if I take this action, what will the world look like afterward? Then you can search over actions internally before committing to one. Autonomous driving is a good example. You really want to roll out futures in your head before acting.

There's also a middle ground that's easy to overlook. Plenty of digital work is still visual: operating a GUI, reading charts, understanding diagrams, editing images or video. In our own work on multimodal models, we kept finding that models which are very fluent in language still fail at surprisingly basic visual things, like spatial relations, orientation, counting, and fine details. That suggests the visual understanding underneath is weaker than the language makes it look. For agents doing computer-use tasks, I think stronger visual grounding, and some notion of how the screen will change after an action, will matter a lot.

So my rough answer is this. For purely symbolic work, language may be enough. For anything embodied, spatial, or where you need to anticipate the consequences of actions in a visual environment, a world model is probably not optional. The open research question is what form it should take. It could be a full pixel-level video generator, or it could be something more abstract that predicts only the parts of the future that matter for the decision.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what kind of work we're asking AI to do. If you look at where language models are already very successful — coding, writing, answering questions, even a lot of reasoning tasks — those are domains where the relevant state of the world is basically captured in text. You don't really need a world model in the visual or physical sense to do well there.

Where I think vision world models become genuinely necessary is when the AI has to interact with the physical world, or predict how it evolves. The obvious case is robotics and embodied agents. If a robot is going to manipulate objects, it needs some notion of what happens next — if I push this cup, will it slide or tip over? That kind of intuitive physics is very hard to get from text alone, because people don't write down most of it. It's the knowledge that's so obvious to humans that it never makes it into the training corpus. So the model has to learn it from visual observation, from video, from interaction.

Autonomous driving is similar — you need to anticipate what other agents will do, how the scene will unfold over the next few seconds. And more broadly, any task involving long-horizon planning in a physical environment benefits from being able to simulate forward: imagine taking an action, predict the consequence, and plan against that prediction rather than just reacting.

There's also an interesting middle ground, which is video understanding itself. Even for passive tasks — understanding a long video, answering questions about what happened — having a predictive model of dynamics helps, because it gives you a strong prior over what's plausible. It's a form of compression, really: if you can predict the next frames, you've understood something about the scene.

That said, I'd push back a little on the idea that we need a full, pixel-perfect world model for everything. Predicting every pixel is probably wasteful — a lot of visual detail is irrelevant to the task. What you really want is a model that predicts the task-relevant aspects of the future at the right level of abstraction. So I suspect the useful world models will be somewhat abstract, maybe operating in a learned latent space rather than in pixels. The open question, and this is something we think about in my group, is how to decide what to keep and what to throw away — which, given the name of this podcast, is really an information bottleneck question.

opus-5.text:
That's a question I find myself going back and forth on, honestly.

My instinct is to be a little skeptical of the strong version of the claim — the idea that you need a full generative world model to do anything useful in the physical world. A lot of tasks that *look* like they demand visual understanding turn out to be solvable with pretty shallow perception plus a strong language prior. If you ask a model to describe a kitchen scene and plan how to make coffee, most of the heavy lifting is coming from text pretraining. The vision part is almost a thin wrapper that grounds a few nouns. And I think we've repeatedly fooled ourselves on benchmarks where the visual input was nearly ablatable — you remove the image and performance barely drops.

Where I do think it becomes genuinely necessary is when the consequences of an action are continuous and you can't enumerate them in language. Contact-rich manipulation is the clearest case. If I'm pushing a stack of objects, whether it topples depends on geometry and friction at a level of precision that no caption captures. You can't say "the mug is near the edge" and recover the dynamics. There you need something that predicts future observations, because the thing you're reasoning about doesn't have a discrete vocabulary.

The other case is anything where you have to act before you've seen the outcome. Navigation in a partially observed space, surgical settings, driving — you need a model that lets you roll forward counterfactuals internally rather than trying things. That's really the functional definition I'd use: a world model is necessary exactly when trial-and-error in the real world is too expensive.

What I'm less convinced of is that pixel-space prediction is the right objective for getting there. Most of the pixels are irrelevant to the decision. We may be spending enormous capacity modeling leaf textures. Something more like a learned latent dynamics model, where the representation is shaped by what matters for control, seems more likely to be what actually works — though I'd say the empirical evidence there is still thinner than the enthusiasm.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it depends on what kind of work you mean. For a lot of what language models do well today, like coding, math, writing, and answering questions, I don't think you need an explicit vision world model. Text is already a very compressed and abstract representation of human knowledge, and the models have done surprisingly well just from that.

Where I think it becomes necessary is anything that has to interact with the physical world. Robotics is the obvious case. If a robot is going to pick something up, navigate a cluttered kitchen, or fold clothes, it has to predict what will happen when it acts. If I push this object, does it slide or tip over? Language is a very lossy channel for that. You can describe a cup falling in words, but the fine-grained details, like the geometry, the contact, and the material, are hard to put into text. That kind of knowledge is much more naturally learned from visual and sensory data.

The other place is planning and reasoning in spatial settings. Humans do a lot of mental simulation. Before I move a couch through a doorway, I imagine it in my head. I think AI systems will need something similar, some internal model of how the visual world evolves, so they can try things out before committing to an action.

I'm also not sure it has to look like a model that generates pixels. Predicting every pixel of the future is probably wasteful, because a lot of that detail doesn't matter for the decision. So the open question for me is what the right representation is. It could be latent, or more abstract, and it needs to capture what's relevant for acting without reconstructing everything. But for embodied tasks, I do think some form of visual world understanding is going to be essential.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think they're most necessary wherever the work involves physical consequences that language doesn't fully capture. If a robot needs to fold a shirt, pour water, or get through a cluttered kitchen, it has to know how the scene will change when it acts, and that's hard to get from text descriptions. The same goes for driving and navigation, where you're constantly predicting what objects will do next.

I'd be careful about the word "world model," though. Predicting every pixel of the future is expensive and often wasteful. What matters is usually a compact representation of the things that affect the task: where objects are, how they're likely to move, what's occluded, what the agent can change. A model that gets those right can plan well without rendering a photorealistic video.

I also don't think we've figured out how to evaluate these systems well. It's easy to produce a generated video that looks convincing and still violates basic physics, so looking good isn't enough. I'd want to see models tested on whether their predictions actually help an agent succeed at a downstream task.

astra-6.text:
I think the clearest case is when an AI needs to act in the physical world. For a robot, recognizing the objects in front of it is only part of the problem. It also needs to anticipate: if I move this object, what else will move? If I take this action, can I get closer to the goal? That’s where I would expect a visual world model to be especially useful—for predicting consequences and planning.

But I wouldn’t say every useful AI system needs one. A lot of work can be described and carried out through language or other structured interfaces. The need becomes stronger when the task depends on spatial relationships, motion, and interactions that are difficult to capture in words.

And the model doesn’t necessarily have to generate a beautiful video of the future. What matters is whether it captures the aspects of the world that let the agent choose a good action.
